tip: 'You should' starts with तुम्हें (tumhein = to you), not तुम – with चाहिए (chahiye), advice points at the person, so they take the to-form.
लेनी (leni), not लेना – the verb before चाहिए matches its object's gender: दवा (dava = medicine) is feminine, so 'to take' becomes लेनी.
There is no verb 'need' here – चीनी चाहिए (cheeni chahiye) is literally 'sugar is wanted'. Noun + चाहिए = need; a verb before चाहिए means 'should'.
और (aur) usually means 'and', but after an amount it means 'more': दो सौ रुपये और (do sau rupaye aur) = two hundred rupees more.
Skills come to you in Hindi: तैरना आता है (tairna aata hai = swimming comes) means 'knows how to swim'. Learned abilities use आना (aana = to come), not सकना.
पड़ेगा (padega) comes from पड़ना (padna = to fall): the duty falls on Nikhil, no choice in it. चाहिए (chahiye) suggests, पड़ना forces.
No extra 'have to' word – करना है (karna hai = is to do) alone means must. The -ना (-na) verb form plus है (hai) carries the whole obligation.
'Is prohibited' is just मना है (mana hai = is forbidden) after the plain verb: फ़ोटो खींचना मना है – no 'it', no passive, nothing else needed.
Impossibility is phrased 'from me': मुझसे (mujhse) + नहीं उठ पाएगा (nahin uth paega = won't get lifted) – the failure comes from your side, and the box बक्सा (baksa) is the subject.
सक (sak) never stands alone – it glues onto the bare verb: बोल सकती है (bol sakti hai = can speak). English puts 'can' before the verb; Hindi attaches it after.
'Should have' just adds था: बोलना चाहिए था (bolna chahiye tha = should have spoken). The past marker sits after चाहिए, nothing else changes.
'Wants us to go' needs a full clause: चाहता है कि (chahta hai ki = wants that) + हम लखनऊ चलें (ham Lakhnau chalen = we go to Lucknow) – never an infinitive like English.
करवाना (karvana) = get it done by someone else: एसी ठीक करवाना (AC theek karvana) is having it repaired, not repairing it yourself – that would be करना (karna).
After शायद (shayad = maybe), the verb shifts to the maybe-form: आ सके (aa sake), not आ सकता है. Uncertainty changes the verb ending itself.
सकना also covers 'might': बारिश हो सकती है (barish ho sakti hai = rain can happen) means it might rain – possibility, not anyone's ability.
'Try on' is wear-and-see: पहनकर देख (pahankar dekh = having worn, see). Hindi tests things by doing the action, then देखना (dekhna = to see).
